claim: At least half of transactions occur online
originalWording: At least half of transactions occur online

sources.title: The Age of Spiritual Machines — Ray Kurzweil (1999)

sourceCaveat: The original book edition has not been independently checked. See the listed source on Sources for attribution limits.

strict.criterion: Online purchase transactions dominate ordinary consumer commerce; retail sales value is the stated empirical proxy.
strict.rationale: US retail e-commerce was only about 3.7% of retail sales in 2009, far from a half-share consumer-commerce interpretation. The 2026 Q2 US share was 17.1%, still below half. This does not decide whether a different denominator including interbank, stock-market or B2B messages might pass.

evidence.title: US Census: Retail e-commerce, fourth quarter 2009
evidence.note: 2009 retail e-commerce share about 3.7% by value. US consumer retail proxy, not all worldwide transactions or number of payments.

evidence.title: US Census: Quarterly retail e-commerce, 2026
evidence.note: Second quarter 2026 e-commerce share 17.1% of retail sales by value. Not B2B, securities trading, or a count of all transactions.

broader.criterion: Online commerce and digital payment networks handle a major, rapidly growing share of everyday consumer transactions.
broader.rationale: E-commerce grew from 3.7% of US retail sales in 2009 to 17.1% in Q2 2026, and digital payment rails process most in-store spending—warranting partial credit. Even charitably, however, brick-and-mortar commerce still accounts for over four-fifths of retail sales, far below half occurring online.
changedConditions: Credits major e-commerce growth and digital payments as partial without treating electronic card swipes as online shopping
